extracted.intended_audience: general readers of classic literature / students of Rabelais
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of an English translation excerpt from Rabelais' Pantagruel (Book IV end and start of Book V). The page is a narrative passage with occasional aphorisms, proverbs, and prescriptive remarks embedded in the fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripatetic rule on problems/questions
rubrics_metrics.description: “the Peripatetics have wisely made a rule that all problems, questions, and doubts which are offered to be solved ought to be certain, clear, and intelligible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel invokes this rule to insist that questions must be well-defined before they are answered; the text immediately uses the rule to probe the meaning of Ponocrates' phrase 'dog-sleep' (which is then defined as sleeping fasting in the sun at noonday). This functions as a guideline for framing inquiries: be precise and intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer appetites with short, demonstrative remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: “My answer shall be short, not to tire you with a long needless train of pedantic cant... you shall be answered to content by signs and gestures. As formerly at Rome, Tarquin the Proud, its last king, sent an answer by signs...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel argues that the belly 'has no ears' and therefore questions about hunger/melancholy etc. should receive brief, practical responses (often by action or demonstration rather than long words). The Tarquin anecdote illustrates communicating by sign/action rather than wordy explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical hours (physicians' schedule for waking, meals, and sleep)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Physicians more properly say that the canonical hours are, To rise at five, to dine at nine, To sup at five, to sleep at nine.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a medical/behavioural guideline for daily rhythm (wake, dine, sup, sleep). The passage contrasts different cultural practices (Persians, Diogenes) and uses the canonical-hours formulation as an asserted proper schedule for bodily health and order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eating/drinking as a remedy to lift spirits and 'raise good weather'
rubrics_metrics.description: Pantagruel's claim that breaking fast and drinking can 'raise the wind' and shorten calms: e.g. 'we have not only shortened the time of the calm, but also much disburthened the ship; not like Aesop's basket, by easing it of the provision, but by breaking our fasts; and that a man is more terrestrial and heavy when fasting than when he has eaten and drank...' and the proverb 'That a cup in the pate Is a mile in the gate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as both a humorous cosmological explanation (sympathy in nature: carousing raises the wind) and practical advice: consuming food and drink makes people more lively and is recommended before a long journey. The passage mixes literal guidance (eat before travel) with satirical mythologizing.
